what_is_strong: The product boundary is clear and consistently enforced: HSConfig is pre-run only, while replay analysis, winrate work, runtime-log analysis, candidate promotion, and after-game tuning stay outside the repo and belong to HSTuner.

The normal operator story is simple at the top level: README points to docs/operator/README.md, `hsconfig configure` is the preferred command, and `reports/operator_summary.json` remains the single operator gate.

The runtime safety model is competent and conservative. The apply gate separates technical validity from semantic richness and allows load-safe initial packages without pretending they are always source-backed strong.
The implementation keeps complexity behind a small CLI surface. Dense policy logic is concentrated in a few modules rather than leaking into many commands or extra runtime dependencies.

The repo is well-defended by tests. Boundary wording, legacy-surface exclusions, installed-skill sync, CLI help, configure/apply behavior, and no-block matrix expectations are all exercised by passing targeted pytest batches.

The repo successfully quarantines most research/archive noise from the normal operator path. `docs/research/README.md` and `docs/research/current-truth.md` explicitly frame research as evidence, not instructions.
what_is_not_optimal: The active skill surface is not truly minimal anymore. `.agents/skills/hsconfig/SKILL.md` and `references/workflow.md` contain large amounts of detailed policy, status taxonomy, matrix-closure truth, and mechanic wording that go beyond a lean trigger-and-entrypoint skill.

Documentation duplication is actively institutionalized by tests. Many assertions in `tests/test_skill_files.py` and `tests/test_docs_active_path.py` require overlapping phrases and repeated detailed concepts across README, operator docs, SKILL.md, and workflow.md, which raises maintenance cost for every wording change.

Legacy `source-informed` terminology is still prominent in active docs and code even though the normal path is now load-safe apply with warnings. That leaves a mild naming-confusion surface between legacy diagnostic compatibility and the actual current operator model.
Research and plan archive size is materially larger than the active operator docs. The archive is mostly contained, but the repo as a whole is not slim in documentation footprint.

The policy core is somewhat over-concentrated in `operator_summary.py`. It is test-backed and working, but nearly 1000 lines in one status-building module is a maintainability pressure point if more terminology or branches are added.
no_block_assessment: The current repo correctly treats no-block as a technical/runtime contract, not a promise of perfect guide strength. A valid package can still be applied when it is load-safe and warnings remain visible.

The live-tested operator model keeps `technical_status=VALID_PACKAGE`, `runtime_load_safe=true`, and `runtime_apply_mode=load_safe_apply` separate from `SOURCE_BACKED_STRONG`, `VALID_BUT_NOT_GUIDE_STRONG`, and config-richness judgments.
Warning-only mechanic visibility, guide-depth gaps, combo uncertainty, and thin-but-load-safe configuration remain non-blocking in the current surface, which matches the intended product boundary.

The remaining no-block weakness is wording complexity, not gate correctness. Legacy `source-informed` language can make the story sound more layered than the runtime gate really is, but the code and tests still enforce the right behavior.
hearthstone_semantic_assessment: Semantic coverage is competent for the current product boundary. The repo visibly handles GlobalValues, Mulligan, per-card CardID outputs, Combo, hero power transforms, choice surfaces, semantic enrichment, and mechanic drift reporting.

The mechanic model is honest instead of over-claiming. It uses direct, identity-gated direct, partial, and warning-only buckets rather than pretending every Hearthstone behavior has a safe runtime lowering.

Modern and awkward mechanic visibility is already present for families such as `kindred`, `tourist`, `starship`, `rewind`, `herald`, `shatter`, `board_position`, `generic_spell_target`, `location_activation`, `secret_timing`, and `generated_entity_random_pool` through reports rather than unsafe runtime writes.

The current semantic gap is not missing whole categories so much as the communication burden around them. The repo is competent, but the active docs spend a lot of space re-explaining nuanced status and closure concepts.
slimness_assessment: The code and dependency footprint are reasonably lean for the job: one runtime dependency, a compact CLI entrypoint, and strong scope boundaries that keep HSTuner and replay concerns out.
The user-facing top-level path is also reasonably lean: short root README, one operator guide, and one preferred command.
The repo is not slim in total documentation mass. `docs/superpowers/plans/` and historical research results are much larger than the active guidance surface, even if they are partially quarantined.

The biggest current inefficiency is active-doc duplication rather than algorithmic inefficiency. The same boundary, status, closure, and mechanic language is repeated across operator docs, skill docs, workflow docs, and tests.
Overall judgment: the skill is competent and maintainable, but only conditionally lean. It is lean in product scope, not lean in active policy wording.
recommended_next_action: Make `docs/operator/README.md` the only detailed active policy manual, then slim `.agents/skills/hsconfig/SKILL.md` and `.agents/skills/hsconfig/references/workflow.md` down to trigger conditions, the preferred command path, the single gate, and hard boundaries; update the doc tests to assert canonical links and a few critical phrases instead of enforcing large duplicated policy blocks and repeated legacy `source-informed` wording.
confidence: high - this audit is grounded in live repo inspection, line-count and term-count checks, installed-skill sync verification, dependency inspection, and two passing targeted pytest batches focused on scope boundaries, active docs, skill sync, CLI, apply gate, and no-block matrix behavior.
